senses.gloss:
ekabera
(‘solitary icon’)
------------------------------------------
Temples of विष्णु are sometimes categorised into two groups: एकबेर temple and bahubera-temple.
In the former group of temples there will be only one (= eka) permanent icon (= बेर) and neither the goddesses (consorts) Śrīdevī and भूदेवी nor the उत्सव-mūrti (processional icon) will be present. All the items of worship are offered only to that single icon.
The expression however, does not apply to the parivāra-देवतास् or attendant deities that may be installed in the appropriate places.
See also BERA.

ekāyana
(‘single [or only] support’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in the उपनिषद्स् in two senses—in its usual sense of ‘the only support’ and in a technical sense, as ‘the science of एथिच्स्’. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.1.2, 4; 7.2.1) it has been used in the latter sense, whereas in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.4.11 and 4.5.12) it is the former that is intended.
By tracing the origin of all objects to their immediate causes, the Upaniṣad comes to the conclusion that ब्रह्मन् is the ultimate cause and support—ekāyana—of the whole world.

ekabhavika doctrine
(‘the doctrine [that many karmas] produce one birth’)
------------------------------------------
The doctrine of कर्म and पुनर्जन्म (rebirth) has been widely accepted by almost all the schools of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्.
There is a long discussion of some of the details of this doctrine in the Vyāsabhāṣya on the Yogasūtras (2.73) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). It is here that this word ‘ekabhavika’ has been introduced and discussed. Literally, it means ‘producing one birth’.
As regards residual कर्म producing rebirth, four alternatives are put forth and only one is accepted as true, ruling out the other three. The alternatives are:
Does one कर्म produce one birth?
Does one कर्म cause several births?
Do several karmas result in several births?
Do several karmas give rise to only one birth?
Since numberless karmas have accumulated from beginningless time, accepting either of the first two alternatives will give rise to a highly confusing situation and people will lose all faith in the karmas prescribed by the śāstras.
The third alternative too has to be ruled out since it is not possible for a जीव (individual सोउल्) to assume several births simultaneously.
Then, by pariśeṣanyāya or the doctrine of elimination of the alternatives, we have to accept only the last alternative as true.
Among the accumulated karmas, one major कर्म, along with several minor karmas which are compatible with the major one, becomes ripe at the time of death and causes the next birth, deciding its जाति (type), āyus (duration of life) and भोग (experiences, good and bad).
See also KARMA.

Ekākṣara Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a small minor Upaniṣad in 13 verses, assigned to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.
It deals with God or ब्रह्मन्, the One (eka = one), who is अक्षर or indestructible and is in the form of a laudatory hymn.
When the sādhaka or the spiritual aspirant meditates upon शिव, along with his consort Umā, in his सहस्रार-चक्र, at the top of the head, and as one with him (Śiva), he realises his identity with शिव who is the One without a second, and the indestructible (akṣara) reality.
This Ekākṣara or the Supreme God, is the creator of this world, the lord of all beings and the primeval being. He is the protector of the world. Though unborn, he is all-pervading. He is the fire and again, he is the sacrifice.
He is हिरण्यगर्भ, the world-सोउल्. He is the sun. He is कुमार or स्कन्द (the commander of the gods). He is इन्द्र, the wielder of the thunderbolt. He is the desires of human beings as also the mantras uttered in sacrificial rites to fulfil them. He is the incarnations like the Varāha (Boar). He is all the वेदस् as also the deity worshipped through the Vedic rites. He it is, again, who has manifested himself as the eleven Rudras.
He is man, woman and child.
In fact there is nothing here that is not the Ekākṣara.
One who knows him, the ancient Lord who has become all, will attain the highest state.
See also UPANIṢADS.

ekadhana
------------------------------------------
In the Somayāgas (Vedic sacrifices using the juice of the सोम creeper for oblations) 3 to 11 earthen jugs are used to keep water collected from a running stream, early in the morning, on the very day of pressing the stalks for the juice. This is later mixed with the सोम juice. The earthen jug used for this purpose has been named ‘ekadhana’. It is rather difficult to give its derivative meaning.

Ekāmra-kṣetra
(‘a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे with one mango tree’)
------------------------------------------
Kāñcīpuram or Kāñcī is one of the seven most holy places of पिल्ग्रिमगे for Hindus.
Once पार्वती, the divine spouse of शिव, incurred his wrath and was cursed by him to become ugly. Later, after repentance, शिव advised her to perform severe austerities to regain him. She sat under a single mango tree (eka = one, āmra = mango tree), regained her beautiful form by the grace of विष्णु and then performed severe austerities as advised. Pleased with her, शिव appeared and accepted her—now known as Kāmākṣī—once again. Hence, this place—the modern Kāñcīpuram—came to be known as Ekāmrakṣetra and the शिव in the temple there, as Ekāmranātha.
There is an ancient mango tree there with a small shrine below it containing the image of पार्वती in meditation
See KĀÑCĪPURAM for details.

ekadaṇḍin
(‘One [who holds] a single staff’)
------------------------------------------
A दण्ड or a staff is an important insignia of a saṁnyāsin (monk). Among such saṁnyāsins called ‘daṇḍis’, there are two types: ekadaṇḍis and tridaṇḍis. The former carry only one (eka = one) staff (of bamboo) where as the latter carry three sticks tied together (tri = three) as one, to facilitate carrying.
The दण्ड stands for दम or self-control. If tridaṇḍa stands for control over body, speech and मिन्द्, ekadaṇḍa stands for control over the मिन्द् only, since that automatically leads to the control of the other two also.
The परमहṁस saṁnyāsins accept a दण्ड at the time of taking सṁन्यास, but break it and discard it in a river, since they are supposed to have attained the highest state wherein they do not need to carry such insignias.

Ekalavya
------------------------------------------
One of the boy-heroes of the Hindu epics who has made an indelible impression upon the minds of one and all, not only for his excellence in the science of archery but also for his gurubhakti—unquestioning devotion to the teacher—is एकलव्य. He was the son of Hiraṇya-धनुस्, the chieftain of the niṣādas, a forest tribe.
When he approached द्रोणाचार्य, the unrivalled preceptor of archery and military sciences, to be accepted as his disciple, the request was rejected since एकलव्य was a śūdra by caste and since the military sciences were the preserve of the kṣattriyas. Undeterred, एकलव्य prepared a clay-image of द्रोणाचार्य, kept it in the field of his practice and started training himself before it, after duly worshipping it since he had mentally accepted द्रोणाचार्य as his गुरु! The intensity of his devotion to the गुरु and the relentless practice made him, very soon, an expert archer.
One day, when the Pāṇḍava princes had come to the forest for hunting, they found that one of their hunting dogs returned with its mouth packed with seven arrows, unable to bark but absolutely unharmed! When the Pāṇḍava princes discovered that it was the hunter-boy एकलव्य’s feat, they were dumbfounded. On learning that द्रोणाचार्य was his ‘teacher’, अर्जुन became upset, since the latter had promised to make him the greatest archer of his times. Being in a fix, द्रोणाचार्य asked एकलव्य to give his right thumb as his ‘fees’. Absolutely unmoved, the boy cut off his right thumb and offered it at his feet! Thus एकलव्य lost his supremacy in archery though he was still good at it, but gained a permanent place in our history.
He is said to have challenged Śrī कृष्ण once for a fight and died at his hands.
See also DROṆĀCĀRYA.

Ekāṣṭakā
(‘The eighth day par excellence’)
------------------------------------------
Performance of certain rites for the benefit of departed ancestors had been an ancient custom in हिन्दुइस्म्. The Ekāṣṭkā rite is one such, performed on the 8th day of the dark fortnight, especially in the month of Māgha (January-February).
See AṢṬAKĀ for details.

ekanakṣatra vivāha
(‘marriage where the नक्षत्र or asterism is the same’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindus consider मर्रिअगे as a saṁskāra or a sacrament. Hence it is much more a religious act than just a social contract.
A factor to be considered before fixing a मर्रिअगे between a boy and a girl is whether the horoscopes of the two are in consonance with each other. One of the most important considerations is the नक्षत्र of birth of the two. Generally, the nakṣatras should be different. If they are the same, then they should be of the auspicious type. For instance, the nakṣatras रोहिणी, आर्द्रा, Makha, Viśākha, पुष्य, Śrāvaṇa, Revatī and Uttarābhādrā are considered highly auspicious. On the other hand, Pūrvābhādra, Dhaniṣṭhā, पुनर्वसु, कृत्तिका, Mṛgaśira, चित्त, हस्त, Uttara-phalgunī, ज्येष्ठा, Pūrvā-ṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā are considered prohibited and hence, inauspicious. Even when मर्रिअगे is performed between persons having a permitted ekanakṣatra, the pādas (quarters) should be different.
Violation of these rules may result in evil consequences including the death of one of the spouses.
See also VIVĀHA.

Ekāgnikāṇḍa
(‘section [dealing with a person having] one fire’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदाङ्गस् or ‘limbs of the वेदस्’ are important subsidiary works that help the student of the वेदस् not only to understand them but also perform correctly the various rites mentioned therein. The कल्पसूत्रस् are one of the six such वेदाङ्गस्.
The Āpastamba Kalpasūtras is one of the oldest among the कल्पसूत्रस् and belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. The 25th and the 26th praśnas or prapāṭhakas or sections of this work are together called Ekāgnikāṇḍa or Mantrapāṭha. Sometimes it is shown as the 31st and the 32nd sections also. There is a well-known commentary by हरदत्त Miśra (A. D. 1100) on this Ekāgnikāṇḍa.
The word itself might have been derived from the fact that all the rites and rituals dealt with here, concern an average householder keeping one fire (= eka + अग्नि), the गार्हपत्य fire or the gṛhyāgnī.
The first chapter comprises 131 mantras spread over 18 khaṇḍas or sections; The second has 356 mantras in 22 khaṇḍas. Almost all the topics described here belong to the field of धर्मशास्त्रस्. They can be briefly stated as follows:
The सṁस्कारस् or sacraments of विवाह (marriage), उपनयन (investiture with the sacred thread and allied rites), समावर्तन (graduation from the गुरु-कुल), rites connected with a pregnant मोथेर् and the new born child, rites connected with the building of a new होउसे, offering of cooked ड़ोओद् prepared from the first agricultural crop, śrāddhas (obsequial rites), various kinds of जप, several religious rituals to offset the evils that befall one in life, other rituals to get certain desires fulfilled and a few other minor rites.
See also ĀPASTAMBA.

ekabhakta
(‘[taking] ड़ोओद् once’)
------------------------------------------
Ekādaśī, the eleventh day of every पक्ष or fortnight of the lunar month, is to be observed as a vrata or religious rite, the main part of it being ड़स्तिन्ग्. This ड़स्तिन्ग् can be of four types, of which the ‘ekabhakta’ is the first. It permits a person who is observing एकादशी, to eat only once (= eka) in 24 hours. The normal time prescribed for this taking of ड़ोओद् is a little after noon.
Ekabhakta can be observed as a vrata independent of एकादशी also. The Mahā-bhārata dilates upon the rewards attained by observing एकभक्त for one year from Mārgaśīrṣa (December) to Kārttika (next November) (Anuśāsanaparva 107.13-126).
See also EKĀDAŚĪ and NAKTA.

Ekacakranagara
------------------------------------------
This was a small town where the Pāṇḍava princes along with their मोथेर् कुन्ती lived for some time, after escaping from the burning होउसे made of lac. A fierce demon Bakāsura by name, was living nearby. He used to attack this little town and would eat up whomsoever he could lay his hands on. Then the people of the town appealed to him not do so, but would themselves send a person everyday as his ड़ोओद्. When कुन्ती came to know of this through her hosts, whose turn it was to send a member of their family, she sent भीम instead. भीम killed the demon thus ridding the town of the great tormentor.

Ekanātha
(A. D. 1533-1606)
------------------------------------------
If Hindu religion and culture have survived the onslaughts of the turbulent vicissitudes in Indian history, it is not a little due to its great saints, especially those of the भक्ति cults. One such bright star that arose in the firmament of western India, in Maharashtra, was एकनाथ (also spelt as Eknāth). With a rare and balanced combination of ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion), he was a true successor of another great saint of Maharashtra, Sant Jñāneśvara (13th century A. D.).
Born in the family of another holy man Bhānudāsa (b. A. D. 1448), at Paiṭhaṇ, एकनाथ lost both his parents early in life. He was brought up by his grand parents. Even in his childhood days he had developed a great love and attraction for that inimitable scripture of devotion to कृष्ण, the Bhāgavata. Inspired by an inner call heard at a nearby शिव temple, he ran away to Devagaḍh, without informing his guardians, and fell at the feet of Janārdana Svāmī, a renowned saint of his times. Janārdana Svāmī (A. D. 1504-1575) was the killedār (officer in-charge of the fort) of the Devagaḍh fort. He was a worshipper of दत्तात्रेय (an aspect of विष्णु) and had had several mystical experiences. He could intuit the greatness of एकनाथ and hence readily accepted him as his disciple. Under his able guidance, एकनाथ speedily progressed in his sādhanās or spiritual practices. By the grace of his गुरु, he could even have visions of दत्तात्रेय.
When Janārdana took एकनाथ on a पिल्ग्रिमगे, he commanded him to translate the Sanskrit Bhāgavata into Marāṭhi verses. एकनाथ undertook the great task with tremendous faith and devotion and successfully completed it in course of time.
His grandparents at Paiṭhaṇ somehow got wind of his whereabouts and appealed to Janārdana to send him back to them. Janārdana not only complied but also commanded एकनाथ to marry and settle down as a householder at Paiṭhaṇ itself. Accordingly, एकनाथ married an extraordinarily pious girl Girijābāī by name, and started living with his grandparents. Being very old, they passed away peacefully soon after.
During his long stay at Paiṭhaṇ he not only spread the message of the Bhāgavata in the local language but also performed many miracles which ultimately silenced his enemies, critics and cavillers. Some of the miracles attributed to him are: being seen in more than one place simultaneously, his dead ancestors appearing physically to eat the ड़ोओद् offered in the śrāddha, postponing the time of death of Kṛṣṇadāsa until he completed his literary work on the Rāmāyaṇa, making the stone image of नन्दि (bull-mount of शिव) in a temple eat grass and so on.
He was also responsible for the renovation of the tomb of the saint Jñāneśvara at आऌअन्दी near Puṇe or Poona.
He passed away in A. D. 1606.

Ekākṣara-Gaṇapati
(‘Gaṇapati[indicated by] one letter’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇapati or गणेश, the elephant faced deity, is one of the most popular of the gods of हिन्दुइस्म्. His बीजाक्षर (the seed-letter containing his power and essence) is ‘gaṁ’. That particular form which is associated with this letter and hence is to be meditated upon while repeating it, is called ‘Ekākṣara-गणपति’. It is one of the eight famous aspects recommended for attaining सिद्धिस् or supernatural powers.
Ekākṣara-गणपति is described as stout and dwarfish. He is red in colour and is seated in पद्मासन or lotus posture. He carries bījāpūra (pomegranate), पाश (lasso) and aṅkuśa (goad) in three hands, the fourth one showing the gesture of varada (bestowing boons).
This form is specially worshipped to attain happiness in life.
See also GAṆAPATI.

ekatāla
(‘of one ताल or span’)
------------------------------------------
See TĀLAMĀNA SYSTEM for details.
In इचोनोग्रफ्य्, this measure is used to prepare images of the lowest class of spirits and kabandhas (headless torsos).
In classical Indian मुसिच्, it is the name of a ताल or measure of time comprising 12 mātrās or instants of time, divided into four equal parts, each consisting of 3 mātrās. These mātrās are represented by such letters as dhī, dhā, na, tṛka and so on. These letters also indicate the places on the percussion instrument where that particular beat is to be struck.

ekadeśin
(‘One who upholds only one aspect’)
------------------------------------------
In the Indian philosophical systems, when a statement is made by the main proponent, objections against it are raised by others opposed to that school. Such an objector usually takes one part (ekadeśa = one part) of the statement of the proponent and tries to criticise it. Such an objector is called ‘ekadeśin’. A more common word for such an objector is ‘pūrvapakṣin’ (one who holds the prima facie view).

Ekādaśinī
(‘that which is eleven times’)
------------------------------------------
See ATIRUDRA.

ekādaśa-gurus
(‘eleven gurus’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu religio-cultural tradition, the गुरु or teacher has an important place. The word itself means ‘one who teaches the scriptures’ like the वेदस्. However, it is used in a much wider sense indicating anyone who deserves respect, like the spiritual preceptor.
The Devala Smṛti lists the fallowing eleven persons (ekādaśa = eleven) as gurus: आचार्य (Vedic teacher), ड़थेर्, elder brother, king, maternal uncle, ड़थेर्-in-law, one who protects or gives shelter, maternal grandfather, paternal grand-ड़थेर्, one who is superior in caste and paternal uncle.

Ekadanta
(‘One who has only one tusk’)
------------------------------------------
Gaṇeśa or गणपति, one of the most popular and widely worshipped Hindu deity, has an elephant’s head and a human body. Out of his two tusks, one is full whereas the other is broken. It is because of this that he is known as ‘Ekadanta’.
The story goes that he lost his tusk in his fight with परशुराम.
Symbolically, the broken tusk stands for this impermanent, imperfect world where as the full tusk stands for the perfect.
In iconographical works एकदन्त गणपति is shown as a special aspect of गणपति, blue-black in colour and with four arms. In them he carries kuṭhāra (hammer), अक्षमाला (rosary), laḍḍu (sweet preparation) and danta (his own broken tusk).
See also GAṆAPATI.

ekaliṅga
(‘[a place where there is] only one शिवलिङ्ग’)
------------------------------------------
Those who perform sādhanās are advised to do them in certain places so that they could get the सिद्धिस् or results (especially psychic powers) more quickly. One such place is called ‘ekaliṅga’ or ‘ekaliṅgakṣetra’. It is defined as a place where there is a शिवलिङ्ग and no other लिङ्ग is found within a radius of five krośas (24 kms. or 15 miles).
The word may stand for कुबेर, the lord of wealth, also since he is said to have only one eye (liṅga = indriya, organ or eye).
In the state of Rajasthan, 19 Kilo-metres (12 miles) from the city of Udaipur, there is a famous temple of Ekaliṅgajī. The शिवलिङ्ग here has four faces on the four sides. This शिवलिङ्ग was the family deity of the rulers of the former princely State of Mewar. There is a lake called Indrasāgar nearby. Spread over the nearby area, are the temples of Ḍuṭeśvara, धारेश्वर, गणेश, Vanavāsinī and लक्ष्मी also.

Ekajaṭā
(‘[The goddess] with a single braid of hair’)
------------------------------------------
One of the aspects of the देवी or the Divine मोथेर्, एकजटा is another name for तारा, also called ‘Ugratārā’. She is so called since her जटा or braided hair sticks upright on the head as a single unit (eka = single). She is the terrific aspect of the देवी that killed Śumbha and Niśumbha (vide Kālikā purāṇa Ch. 60).
She is probably the Hindu edition of a Buddhist goddess of the Vajrayāna school.
The works Mantramahodadhi and Sādhanamālā contain details of her मन्त्र and procedure of worship.
See also UGRATĀRĀ.

ekavākyatā
(‘single sentence-ness’)
------------------------------------------
While interpreting the various passages from the वेदस् and the उपनिषद्स्, the ancient and medieval commentators have exercised great care. One of the principles they have adopted in their commentaries and interpretations is ‘ekavākyatā’.
A vākya or a sentence is not just an aggregate of words, grammatically or syntactically connected. It should also convey sense. When the sense is not complete and needs further clarification, which is given in one or two or more sentences, all these sentences together will then have ‘ekavākyatā.’
For instance, take these sentences:
parvato vahnimān (There is fire in the hill.)
dhūmāt (Because smoke is seen there.)
yatra yatra dhūmaḥ, tatra tatra vahniḥ (wherever there is smoke, there is fire.)
There are three sentences here. Each one of them conveys a different idea. But all the three put together produce a single knowledge in our मिन्द्, viz., that there is fire on the hill. Thus there is एकवाक्यता in all these three statements.

Ekapādamūrti
(‘image with one leg’)
------------------------------------------
God has sometimes been described in the Hindu scriptures as Ekapāt or Ekapādaḥ since the manifested universe is only a quarter (pāda = quarter) of him. The word is applied to both शिव and विष्णु. ‘Ajaikapāt’ is one of the epithets of शिव, used even in the Ṛgveda (6.50.14; 10.64.4).
The एकपादमूर्ति is actually the iconographic representation of the Vedic concept of शिव as Ajaikapāt. In this form he has only one leg. He is described as luminous like a million suns, three-eyed and four-armed, in which he carries टङ्क (chisel) and Mṛga (antelope). He is exhi-biting the abhaya as also the varada mudrās in the other two hands.
‘Ekapāda’ (one leg) signifies the Supreme Godhead as the sole support of the whole universe.

Ekādaśa-Rudras
(‘The group of eleven Rudras’)
------------------------------------------
Though रुद्र/Śiva has been projected as one of the trinity, representing the destructive aspect of God, there are also minor deities called Rudras who are sometimes listed as eight and sometimes as eleven. They may be gaṇadevatās, attendants of शिव.
The following are some of the deities common to the different lists of eleven Rudras found in the epics and the पुराणस्: Ajaikapāt, Ahirbudhnya, Pināki, Tryambaka, Hara, Aparājita, Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, and others.
Almost all these names are those of रुद्र/Śiva himself.

ekajīvavāda
(‘the view [that there is only] one सोउल्’)
------------------------------------------
Śaṅkara (A. D. 788-820) gave only the main outlines of Advaita philosophy in his writings. However, many gaps regarding the nature of the जीव, nature and locus of अविद्या and māyā, the need to accept a greater degree of reality for the world to facilitate the practice of Vedāntic sādhanās had to be filled up. Later writers who dealt with these aspects developed various schools of Advaita, generally known now as ‘Post-शङ्कर Advaita’.
One such school is the ‘ekajīvavāda’ of Prakāśānanda (A. D. 15th/16th century) propounded in his famous work Vedānta-सिद्धान्त-muktāvalī. According to this theory there is only one जीव (eka = one) bound by one अविद्या (nescience). Hence when his अविद्या is destroyed, he is liberated. There is none else in bondage, to be liberated, since the entire world and all the other jīvas are only figments of his imagination brought about by his अविद्या!
This जीव is sometimes identified with हिरण्यगर्भ, the world सोउल्.
This school did not become popular. Only one writer of the later period, Jñānottama Bhaṭṭārka, has supported it in his Vidyāśrī, a subcommentary on the Brahmasūtras.
See also DṚṢṬI-सृष्टि-VĀDA.

Ekāha
(‘of one day’s [duration]’)
------------------------------------------
Any सोम sacrifice of one day’s duration (eka = one, ahan = day) is called ‘Ekāha’. It is distinguished from अहीन and Sattra which are of longer duration. For instance, अग्निष्टोम sacrifice, which is a part of ज्योतिष्टोम, is an एकाह. The main rite of pressing सोम juice is performed here in one day.

ekādaśī
(‘the eleventh [day])
------------------------------------------
Even in the मिन्द् of an average ignorant Hindu, एकादशी and उपवास (fasting) have practically become synonymous! ड़स्तिन्ग् as a spiritual discipline—whether as an expiation for sins committed or for gaining self-control—has been an age-old practice. When ड़स्तिन्ग् reduces the sway of the flesh over the मिन्द्, it is much easier to control it and direct it towards God, so that it can ‘live near him’. In fact, this is the literal meaning of the word ‘upavāsa’ (upa = near, vāsa = living).
Ekādaśī (eleventh day in both halves of the lunar month—śuklapakṣa and kṛṣṇapakṣa) can be observed just as a spiritual discipline or as a ‘vrata’ with all the concomitant rules. Again, if observed as a vrata, it can be ‘nitya’ (compulsory) or ‘kāmya’ (motivated by desires). In the former case only śukla ekādaśīs need be observed. As a kāmya-vrata, it can be observed on both the days.
Whenever it is undertaken as a vrata, apart from the ड़स्तिन्ग्, सङ्कल्प (resolve), worship of विष्णु and jāgaraṇa (keeping vigil in the night) become obligatory. It is interesting to note that एकादशी is also called “Harivāsara’ (Hari’s or विष्णु’s day) and only worship of विष्णु has been prescribed. In fact, for the Vaiṣṇavas (those belonging to the cult of विष्णु) it is compulsory! Since ड़स्तिन्ग् and keeping vigil on the Māsaśivarātri days (caturdaśī of kṛṣṇapakṣa in every month) was compulsory for the Śaivas, they may have been omitted from its purview.
The पुराणस् and the धर्मशास्त्रस्, though they prohibit the partaking of cooked ड़ोओद् on एकादशी days, have made many concessions to the general human weakness towards ड़ोओद्. If one eats only once in the day around noon, it is called ‘ekabhukta;’ if it is only in the night, it is ‘nakta;’ if the ड़ोओद् is taken once a day, only when it is got by chance, without begging for it, it is ‘ayācita.’ The last, however, seems to apply only to prāyaś-cittas or expiations for sins.
In all, there are 24 ekādaśīs in a lunar year. They are given different names as follows:
Month Bright-fortnight Dark-fortnight
Caitra Kāmadā Varūthinī
Vaiśākha Mohinī Aparā
Jyeṣṭha Nirjalā Yoginī
Āṣāḍha Śayanī Kāmikā
Śrāvaṇa Putradā Ajā
Bhādrapada Parivartinī Indirā
Āśvina Pāśāṅkuśā Ramā

Among these, however, आषाढ śukla एकादशी called ‘Śayanī’ and Kārttika śukla एकादशी named as ‘Prabodhinī’ are important since विष्णु is supposed to sleep on the Śayanī day and wake up on the Prabodhinī day, as the very names indicate. Śayanī is also called ‘Prathamaikādaśī’. A very big festival is held at Phaṇḍarāpur of Maharashtra on this day. Devotees (called Vārkarīs) come from different parts and assemble in thousands to do bhajans (devotional singing).
The एकादशी of Mārgaśira-śukla-पक्ष is observed as गीता Jayantī. It is on this day that Śrī कृष्ण taught the Bhagavadgītā to अर्जुन on the battle-field of कुरुक्षेत्र, before the महाभारत war. Apart from ड़स्तिन्ग् and worship of the Gītācārya कृष्ण, there will be a ceremonial chanting of the text and some times, discourses expounding the same.
The Pauṣa-śukla-एकादशी is well-known as वैकुण्ठ-एकादशी. On this day, thousands of people gather in विष्णु temples. One of the main doors called ‘Vaikuṇṭha-द्वार’ which is normally kept closed throughout the year, is thrown open on this day. The devotees who pass through this door for the darśan of the Lord are believed to go to वैकुण्ठ, the abode of विष्णु. It is said that, long back, the devotee रुक्माङ्गद who was being forced by an ogress to break his एकादशी fast, against the norms of the vrata, was saved by विष्णु and was taken to वैकुण्ठ on this day. Hence the name. There is a very big festival on this day at the रङ्गनाथ temple of श्रीरङ्गम् in Tamil Nadu, which goes on for 21 days.

ekamukhaliṅga
(‘one-faced लिङ्ग’)
------------------------------------------
Śiva, the god of dissolution of the Hindu Trinity, is worshipped invariably in the form of a लिङ्ग or an emblem of rounded surface. (See LIṄGA for details.) One of the several varieties of liṅgas is the mānuṣaliṅga, a लिङ्ग prepared by human beings, as per the directions given in the आगमस् like Ajitāgama and Supra-bhedāgama.
Śiva with one faceIn the मुखलिङ्ग of this variety, one or more mukhas or faces of शिव are carved on the पूजाभाग (the cylindrical part seen above the ground). If there is only one mukha, it is then called ‘ekamukhaliṅga’. It is carved on the round पूजाभाग facing the main door of the shrine, and occupying 120 degrees of space. Its height should be more than one हस्त or ताल but less than five tālas.
See also MUKHALIṄGA and TĀLAMĀNA SYSTEM.

Ekānaṁśā
(‘One who is without parts’)
------------------------------------------
Ekānaṁśā is a folk goddess who is identified with दुर्गा, who was the daughter of नन्द and यशोदा. It was she who was exchanged for baby कृष्ण. She escaped from the clutches of the tyrant कṁस, warned him of his approaching death and disappeared.
She is also described as the tribal divinity of the Vṛṣṇi clan, of कृष्ण-Vāsu-deva. She again, is pictured as सुभद्रा, the sister of बलराम and कृष्ण.
Iconographical representations show her in the standing posture, with two arms, one resting on the loins and the other holding a lotus.

ekāntadharma
(‘a धर्म [which has only] one end’)
------------------------------------------
In the devotional scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म् (vide नारद Bhaktisūtras 70), devotees of God, of the highest type, are called ‘ekāntins’. It means those devotees whose only end and aim of life is God (eka = one, anta = end). Their devotion and consequent characteristics manifested there of can be described as ‘ekānta-धर्म’.
Some of these are: shedding tears in the name of God, being overcome by devotion; hearty conversations with other devotees on topics related to God and spiritual disciplines; visiting places of पिल्ग्रिमगे; performing scripture-ordained actions as a model for others; deep immersion in the thoughts of God; not making any distinction based on caste, learning, pedigree, wealth and so on, while dealing with others.
